english: Date: April 7, 1955 From: Genetic Engineer E. Malakhova To: Secretary A. Uvarov  THIS MESSAGE HAS BEEN REDIRECTED TO THE SECURITY TERMINAL DUE TO THE USE OF WORDS MARKED BY THE CENSORSHIP FILTER  Listen, I didn't come here to teach biology, I came here to run a department. Please tell all those "conquerors" of new plants very clearly that, no matter what we do to them, tropical plants will not be able to generate the amount of oxygen needed for terraforming. Yes, equatorial forests are the largest producers of oxygen on the planet, but they're also its largest consumers. Can they maintain a balance? Sure. Can they create a new system? No way. What you really need are phytoplankton. Surprise! They're the main producer of oxygen on Earth. But those guys would know that if they hadn't been daydreaming about the stars in biology class.

Date: April 7, 1955 From: Senior Roboticist A. Yshtelbyev To: Vavilov Archivist M. Orlikova  Read this translation of an article from the magazine "National Geology" and ask Vavilov's soil experts what kind of biting response we can give our overseas "comrades." "Without a doubt, Burav robots are one of the greatest achievements of Soviet science. According to published data, the Burav is one of just a few Soviet designs that are not supplied to us in the US or any other country. We have no precise data, but we believe there are less than two dozens of them in all the Soviet countries combined. Mighty steel worms capable of chewing through black soil and mountainous mineral veins with ease, they can create hundreds of square meters of useful underground space for Soviet facilities per day. It's hard to imagine how many complexes already exist beneath the surface of the Soviet Union. On the surface, the Burav would seem to be a perfect device. However, the Buravs have one flaw: the effect they have on the soil. Due to their secrecy, Buravs rarely appear above ground, so they move from one construction site to the next via the shortest route possible: underground. According to independent data obtained by geologists, the number of caverns, cavities, and caves in the USSR has been increasing for years now. But what about the massive incidents of soil collapse in Yamala? Buravs are a tremendous environmental threat that could alter the climates of entire regions in the future."

Date: Sverdlov 1, 1984 From: G. Svobodin to: G. Svobodin  Hypothetically speaking, thanks to today's discovery of supplementary biphoton quantum entanglement, I can actually send this letter into the past—say, thirty years ago—to myself, at this very terminal. Date: December 1, 1954 From: Academy of Consequences Secretary's Office To: Vavilov Archivist D. Semushev   Re: your request for excerpts about the Facility from foreign media.  "Washington Post," May 8, 1955, article: "The Soviet Union's Steel Frame" by Tom Wolfe "Universal roboticization in the Soviet Union can be considered a most curious case of modern hypocrisy. Ignoring any populist questions about whether or not robots that pass the Turing test have personal identities, I am merely pointing out how absurd, and at the same time sinister, the widespread use of this workforce is. Judge for yourselves—a nation whose guiding light is an ideology that embraced equality and strives to end the exploitation of workers and peasants by capital has now subordinated an entire army of soulless machines that can satisfy its every whim. I don't know anything about Kollektiv 2.0, but I'd say the Soviet Union is Capitalism 2.0 writ large. The only question is when these robots will demand equal rights for themselves, and how bloody the revolution will be."

Date: June 1, 1955 From: M. Ilyushin To: Academy, News Prediction Dept.  The Raven-1 satellite was launched into orbit, but we were immediately notified that it had malfunctioned. That's the official version, anyway. The unofficial version is more complicated—the Plyusch samples on the orbiting satellite began to behave in a completely unexpected fashion in zero gravity and independently (!) terminated communications with Earth. Two years later, in 1957, we're planning to send a remote-controlled module disguised as another satellite to shed some light on these events, but until then, Raven-1 will be described as a failed, shuttered project in all official documents.

Date: June 1, 1955 From: Vavilov Complex Manager V. Vavilov To: Vavilov Archivist D. Semushev  Dear Comrade Semushev, I am utterly stunned by your careless attitude to the censorship of materials that have been published following your consultation in a number of periodicals.  References to the complex as cut off from real life or having a poor connection to our production facilities are simply false. Vavilov Complex is, first and foremost, a scientific institution that operates according to a specific plan. Our theoretical work is bound up in the most substantial way with practical issues related to seed cultivation and the Facility's future designs. A man would have to be blind to deny the enormous accomplishments Vavilov's team has made in so little time and under such trying circumstances. The Institute's research is laying the foundation necessary to develop a real-world project to conquer new worlds! Going forward, please be more mindful of how our work is depicted in print.

Date: March 10, 1955 From: Vavilov Archivist D. Semushev To: Vavilov Archive Dept.  "On the Acceleration of Evolution" Despite all their talent and the indisputable success achieved by Vavilov's research assistants, there is a concern regarding an issue that, while predictable, can only be confirmed in practice. This problem is more profound than preparing seeds for inhospitable conditions on other planets. Unlike scientists, evolutionary mechanisms do not make predictions or evaluate risk. They simply function, culling the weak and rewarding the strong. Dozens or even hundreds of factors will affect the growth and development of our cultures, so it makes sense to suggest that, while working with the genetics of plants, we should begin by breeding them for faster growth and renewal rather than trying to foresee every minor detail about them.  We just need to give evolution a shot in the arm, and it'll do the rest for us. Which is how it's always been, by the way.

Date: May 11, 1955 From: Publishing Dept. To: Printing Archive  "Are you willing to die? Then you're our man!"  Speaker: Despite the march of progress, one fact remains: flying to the Red Planet is a risky, dangerous proposition.   Reporter: Who are the people who will bring the light of humanity to Mars for us all?  Speaker: I think that the first trips to Mars will be very, very dangerous. The risk of a lethal outcome will be high. But it can't be helped. Are you willing to die? Then you're our man.   Reporter: How would you describe this mission?  Speaker: I think it's the most inspiring thing I could possibly imagine. Life should be something more than just solving everyday problems. When you wake up in the morning, you should think about the future with ecstasy. You should feel inspired and love life.

Date: January 11, 1954 From: Professor Lebedev To: Lab Assistant M. Klimov (ARCHIVE)  Comrade Klimov, do you seriously want to get data on an alternative timeline in which the Third Reich never invented the V-2 rocket? You want to know how the world would be different? Okay, I'll tell you. It wouldn't! Do you know why? Because the invention of new weapons is called an "arms race" for a reason! If it's a race, that means someone has to come in first. In our history, the Germans came in first (although it didn't particularly help them), but the American were nipping at their heels, as were we and the Brits. Yes, the V-2 had an astonishing influence on missile design and the space program, but it was just a matter of time. Can you tell me who invented the radio? Was it Popov? Marconi? Hertz? Tesla? Do you know what's really interesting? What would have happened if the damn Fascists hadn't invented that "plague" of theirs and mowed down half the world's population?!  From now on, don't bother the Alternate Prediction Department with childish questions in the vein of "who'd win in a fight, a shark or a bear?"  P.S. The bear, obviously.

Date: January 12, 1955 From: Pavlov Complex Manager I. Pavlov To: Pavlov Cultural Archivist V. Nikitin  Progress by leaps and bounds has become typical of humanity in this challenging 20th century. Against the background of tremendous inequality, breakthroughs in science and technology can seem not just astonishing, but even insulting. But this is a sociological and political matter. Right now I want to contemplate the issue of the individual, who, feeling himself in a state of accelerated free-fall, is being flung forward faster and faster by progress. Much like the pseudo-scientific fears voiced when the railroads were being built, when the suggestion was actually made that the sight of the landscape whizzing by at 50 kilometers per hour would drive passengers mad, I am beset by similar predictions. Just 25 years ago more than half of all Soviet citizens were illiterate. Today, we are flying into space. What awaits us tomorrow? Will we have time to catch our breath before our next great leap?

Date: March 13, 1955 From: Academy of Consequences Secretary's Office To: Vavilov Archivist D. Semushev  Despite its secrecy, Argentum ("silver" in Latin) has already become the stuff of legend in a number of European and American publications. Journalists are surprised by its extremely small staff, its incredible training and equipment, and its name, which is very atypical of the Soviet Union (you've got to admit, compared to abbreviations like SMERSH and NKVD, it comes off as odd and clumsy). Rumors vary. The squad's soldiers are described either as enormous red-eyed bears who eat children or athletic blond supermen, one look at whom would have driven Hitler to dissolve the Reich and admit the German Übermensch's defeat.  They are a mystery and will remain one, but we can say this much for certain: Argentum is currently the best-trained special forces squad on Earth. And, given the Soviet Union's plans, it could become the best-trained squad in the Solar System before long.

Date: September 14, 1953 From: Publishing Dept. To: Printing Archive  "The time has come to acknowledge that we are careening into the future at an amazing speed. Our scientific machine is running at full capacity, and the most talented Soviet citizens are working day and night to advance the cause of progress. But what of evolution? It remains in the distant past. The 1917 revolution demonstrated that it was possible to tear down the old and erect the new in its place. The same goes for the decrepit, monarchistic phenomenon of evolution. Now man is not just the pinnacle of creation, but a creator himself, and he has the ability and the right to alter himself in accordance with his desires. Gills for divers, wings for first responders, flame-retardant skin for firemen—this is just a small sample of what awaits us in the near future. We are no longer grist for the mill of natural selection—we ARE natural selection." From Comrade Sechenov's lecture to the Soviet Academy of Sciences, 1953

Date: February 14, 1955 From: Publishing Dept. To: Printing Archive  Andrey Rayanovsky's Unknown Feat (draft of an article)  For a long time, Andrey Rayanovsky's name was spoken of with contempt and dismay in Soviet scientific circles. As a capitalist and idealist who fled the Soviet Union and a vocal critic of the Party's authority and the ideals of communism, it was obvious that a good relationship with him was simply impossible. However, later, when Rayanovsky tellingly grew disillusioned with American ideals, his rhetoric changed, and his relationship to the Motherland changed along with it. It goes without saying that this move led to a hue and cry in the West and genuine glee in Rayanovsky's homeland. Nowadays Andrey Rayanovsky has successfully developed his deep-sea dwelling project with the aid of underwater engineers from Sakhalin and is considered a true friend of Soviet science and Facility 3826.

Date: October 15, 1954 From: Pavlov Debate Club President N. Azarova to: archive terminal  Speaker: When I give talks in the Soviet Union and allied countries, I am often asked whether it makes sense to focus scientific progress on making fundamental changes to the human race. We could, for example, teach people to change the properties of their skin in order to make it more resistant to heat or cold, or regrow lost limbs like certain reptiles, or control their biochemistry on a basic level. In other words, to rephrase a well-known thesis, should we strive for "evolution in the individual?"  From the room: skeptical laughter  Speaker: My answer is "no." I admit that this is a defeatist attitude. But my objection does not lie in some bourgeois conception of man as the pinnacle of creation. We have access to powerful technology, and yet we should not alter ourselves to suit our environment. This would be a step backwards. Instead, we must perfect science in order to fully subjugate nature itself, whether it be here on Earth, or somewhere else.

Date: March 18, 1955 From: Junior Genetic Engineer E. Malakhova To: Senior Genetic Engineer A. Raguzin  Who cares about "martian potatoes" or "moon wheat?" You're coming up with really boring names. Trust me, it matters. What if we fly off to another solar system, like Aldebaran or whatever—I don't know, I'm no expert on that stuff—and then we plant our magnificent, non-picky sunflower on a planet there, but then it turns out it's not a sunflower at all! Because there's no Sun! So now it's an Aldebaran flower! Think about that. And we should think about blueberries too, since they won't even be blue on Mars. We could call them "redberries," but that's no good... and "pinkberries" just sounds weird to me.

Date: March 18, 1955 From: Stenography Dept. To: ARCHIVE  Excerpt from a paper by Lebedev  In response to those who are curious about the Radio of the Future, yes, we really can listen to radio broadcasts from the future. Literally. How does it work? If you read any of my previous papers, you'll find out. But you aren't really interested in the technical details, are you? You're interested in what it can do for you. You want to know if you can buy a lottery ticket knowing that it will win, or avoid a nuclear holocaust. Am I right? It's not that simple. What we are hearing is a PROBABLE future, what could happen in ten, thirty, or fifty years based on what's happening right now. But we have never—I repeat, never—heard the same broadcast twice. A week ago the Soviet Union crumbled in 1989 and ceased to exist as a country. This morning we heard a presentation by the general secretary of the Communist Party from 1999. One day we intercepted an emergency message about the launch of nuclear missiles in 1976... I was horrified. The future DOES NOT EXIST YET. Please remember that. All we can hear is an echo of an infinite quantumized multivariance and extract the most frequently repeated tendencies from it. What we will actually see tomorrow is entirely in our hands.

Date: May 19, 1955 From: Lab Supervisor A. Privalov To: Senior Lab Assistant E. Debaltovskaya  Here's my opinion on your article "On the Culture of Instant Messaging." All in all, I think it's well written—it's succinct, and it does a good job of explaining the concept of developing faster ways to transmit text. The comparison to mail, then the telegraph, then the telephone, and then, finally, the terminal system, is quite good.  However, your frivolous dalliance with depicting emotions via text seems entirely out of place, or even theatrical. How do you imagine people will use punctuation to fill a text-based message with emotional content? People still don't even understand the difference between a dash and a hyphen, or a comma and a semicolon, and you want them to start using these characters to communicate their mood? It's truly absurd. Get rid of it.

Date: May 19, 1955 From: Lab Assistant M. Iosipova To: Senior Lab Assistant E. Debaltovskaya   Ekaterina, I read what you wrote about using a colon and a parenthesis to make a smiley face. It's a cute idea, but Privalov will never approve something like that. I think you'd be better off doing it a different way. Remember how people used to abbreviate words in telegrams? Maybe if you want to show you're happy, you could write "HAP," and if you feel sad, you could just write "SAD." Think it over. XOXO, Maria

Date: November 19, 1954 From: Lab Supervisor A. Privalov To: Senior Lab Assistant E. Debaltovskaya  From a comprehensive article from "Technology for Kids" about the Facility "In the West, smart, educated people call us 'homo sovieticus.' They're proud to have discovered this type of person, so they came up with this nice name. They also use this name to humiliate us and put us down. They don't realize we've done something more: we were the first to breed this type of person, but in the West all they can do is come up with new words for things, and they think this contribution to history is much more important than our accomplishments. The West's high opinion of itself is deserving of ridicule." P.S. At Sechenov's request, find references to "homo sovieticus" throughout the entire database and change it to "homo futurum" in every instance.

Date: November 19, 1954 From: Pavlov Debate Club President N. Azarova To: archive terminal  Excerpt from debate club minutes  Speaker 1: Maintaining the high level of technology Soviet science has achieved obviously requires people of profound intellect. That is why the fear that a situation could arise in which technology allows society to become stupider is irrational. Otherwise this level of technology would be ultimately unsustainable. Topic: The Atomic Heart Project Speaker: Dr. Dmitry Sechenov  Welcome, Comrades. In 1951, the capitalist imperialism of the United States, consumed by hatred and envy for the Soviet Union's magnificent scientific achievements, declared the launch of the global Energy for All program. In essence, this program is just as hypocritical as the capitalist system itself. Hiding behind a facade of lofty ideals, the capitalists strive for worldwide hegemony, the suppression of all independence other than their own, and the eradication of those who do not share their values.  At first glance, Energy for All seems incredibly noble: fifty nuclear power stations will be constructed throughout the United States in order to provide every American citizen with cheap and available electricity. But the United States' capitalist regime is, as always, hiding its true face, twisted into the beastly grin of imperialism, behind a mask of magnanimity. In addition to these power stations, the United States is also secretly building a network of underground silos and hangars for launching nuclear missiles and housing strategic bombers armed with nuclear bombs.  The Americans' goal is simple: once the Soviet Union believes their claims of peace and friendship, it will let down its guard, and the American military machine will strike, destroying the Soviet Union and the entire communist way of life with a cowardly sneak attack! But the Soviet Union isn't one to sit on its hands and wait while our enemies regroup and swell their ranks, hiding nuclear weapons underground where we cannot eliminate them from orbit. Nor is the Soviet Union one to back down or run from another nation's might. In response to the American threat, Facility 3826 has developed its own project designed not only to protect the Soviet Union, but also to rid the world once and for all of the very possibility of such a bloodbath. The president of the United States once called Energy for All America's "atomic heart." Given the profound guile and hypocrisy of American capitalism, this name reflects the essence of the global threat developed by the United States all too well. For this reason, our project, which will counteract the Americans' deadly machinations, has co-opted their leader's metaphor. Our Atomic Heart will return honestly and integrity to America!  The Atomic Heart project is made up of several sequential steps:  - Design and build civilian robots with no weapons or other signs of a potential military application. These robots have been designed to be independent of their software. Any owner can install any software onto them they like. On the outside, the robots seems to be perfectly harmless, safe, and friendly. But in reality, they are equipped with highly effective hand-to-hand combat techniques and can use civilian equipment as lethal weapons.  - Stage two of this project requires that Soviet civilian robots be seen by the entire world as humanitarian goods. We have already implemented this strategy via the United Nations. Since receiving the status of humanitarian goods, Soviet robots have begun to spread throughout the entire world free of charge, which has given a powerful impetus to the further development of the Atomic Heart project. Profit-hungry American capitalists are flooding their country with our robots. A free robotic workforce is the dream of every capitalist usurper, and none of them has hesitated to obtain as many Soviet robots as possible.  - During stage three, the Soviet Union has made obtaining free robots as easy as possible for our foreign customers. American businesses, for one, have already imported over one hundred million Soviet civilian robots of various models. Many of these are used at facilities related to Energy for All, i.e. American power stations and missile silos. There, our robots, on which American special forces have installed their own software, maintain, service, and operate nuclear facilities. The first objective of the Atomic Heart project has thus been accomplished.  - During the final phase of the project, civilian robots will be switched form civilian operation to combat mode. They will then capture all key components of the infrastructure of the United States. This will become possible with the launch of Kollektiv 2.0, which will unite all Soviet robots into a unified Neuropolymer network that requires no radio signals, digital protocols, or other electronics. All Soviet robots will be able to receive and successfully carry out our commands. Their attack will be sudden, and it will happen everywhere, all at once, down to the second. The enemy will be taken completely by surprise, and they will be eradicated. The American working class will be liberated from the oppression of global capitalism, and the very notion of capitalism will be lost in the waters of Lethe.  The launch of Kollektiv 2.0 is only two months away. In just two months, a new, progressive human race will toss capitalism into the dustbin of history, cast off the tyrants' yoke, and begin its march into the future. The world will never be the same, comrades!
